storyboard.claim: A human lizard-brain reaction can still be a failure of character.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack alone, worried face, thinking — he knows what he did was wrong even if it was instinctive.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Direct response to context beats 117-119 defending Jack's Halloween moment.
storyboard.addedInformation: Grants the human excuse, then takes it back — character is the standard above instinct.

storyboard.claim: The book does not grade on a curve — the impact on August is identical no matter how old Jack is.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Spectrum from Age 10 to Age 30 with the midpoint marked.
storyboard.onScreenText: The pain lands the same whether Jack is ten or thirty
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the failure verdict by removing the youth excuse.
storyboard.addedInformation: Auggie's slump beneath the diagram grounds the abstract argument in a body.

storyboard.claim: Jack's betrayal breaks Auggie's heart; Jack must spend the rest of the book earning redemption.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie slumped in the foreground, Jack behind him worried — the damage between them visible in their posture.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Consequence of the 'failure of character' verdict — names the narrative cost.
storyboard.addedInformation: The word 'earning' implies ongoing effort, not a single apology.

storyboard.claim: Jack must build the moral backbone he lacked on Halloween.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack thinking, worried — internally reckoning with what he didn't do.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Confirms the host's concession that Jack failed, but points forward to redemption arc.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: 'build' implies future growth; the viewer only sees the present deficit.

storyboard.claim: Jack's failure didn't happen in a vacuum — Julian is the architect pulling the strings of the herd.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian pointing with a smirk — sinister charm, the engineer of social pressure.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts attention from Jack's weakness to Julian's active design.
storyboard.addedInformation: Smirk (not happy) signals threat, not friendliness.

storyboard.claim: Julian's notes and whispers are a master class in under-the-radar bullying.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian holding notes with a smirk — the paper weapon he deploys invisibly.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Zooms in on Julian's specific method after naming him the architect.
storyboard.addedInformation: The notes icon is literal — Julian's actual instrument — and the callout carries the judgment.

storyboard.claim: It's February — the conflict in fifth grade is at its absolute peak.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian in the school corridor (street set = hallway) with smirk — the apex of his campaign.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets the scene for the locker-room incident about to be described.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the month February is implied by context only.

storyboard.claim: Julian and friends play monkey-in-the-middle using Jack's gym shorts as the ball.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian grabbing, Jack struggling — two bodies, the humiliation made physical.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: First concrete example of Julian's locker-room tactics.
storyboard.addedInformation: Grabbing action with two cast members reads as grabbing/seizing, which fits the tossing game.

storyboard.claim: Jack takes it without reacting — he knows the rules of engagement and won't give Julian the satisfaction.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack blank-faced and still — apathy/numbness as a strategic survival response.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Jack's internal response to the gym-shorts humiliation.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank reads as apathy/numbness — here it is deliberate suppression, which is close enough.

storyboard.claim: If Julian bullied Auggie directly and got caught, adults would intervene — so he stays indirect.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian in foreground smirking; Tushman behind him — the authority Julian is carefully evading.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the strategic logic behind Julian targeting Jack rather than Auggie directly.
storyboard.addedInformation: Tushman's presence makes the adult-supervision constraint visible.

storyboard.claim: Julian redirects to Jack the ally and starts slipping notes into their lockers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian holding a note with a smirk in the hallway — the locker-note campaign in action.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The tactical escalation after establishing why Julian won't attack Auggie directly.
storyboard.addedInformation: Notes icon is literal; callout names the method precisely.

callout.text: Those notes are cruelty to August

storyboard.claim: The same notes are juvenile to Jack but vicious targeted hate speech to Auggie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie holding a note, sad — the weight of words that land differently on him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reveals the asymmetry: Jack reads banter, Auggie reads cruelty.
storyboard.addedInformation: Jack's presence in cast signals the contrast even without showing his lighter reaction.

storyboard.claim: The vicious language ('Freak! Orc!') thrives because it operates in the adults' blind spots.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie slumped and afraid — absorbing hate speech no teacher witnesses.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the systemic condition that makes Julian's campaign possible.
storyboard.addedInformation: Afraid face is correct: receiving 'Get out of our school' is terror, not shock.

storyboard.claim: Teachers don't see the notes through locker vents or the gym shorts tossed when backs are turned.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Tushman neutral in the hallway — oblivious — Julian behind him smirking.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Illustrates the blind-spots mechanism with the specific adult who should see.
storyboard.addedInformation: Tushman first in cast because the sentence is about adult failure to see.

storyboard.claim: A detail the narrator loves: within the dark ecosystem, Auggie and Jack show agency.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie and Jack talking, surprised/energized — the pivot from victim to actor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the corner from cataloguing Julian's cruelty to the resistance that comes next.
storyboard.addedInformation: Surprised face reads as revelation/energy, matching the narrator's 'I absolutely love' tone.

storyboard.claim: Jack and Auggie don't just take it — they invent the fictional girl named Bula and fight back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack and Auggie talking with genuine happy energy — co-conspirators, not victims.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers on the 'agency' pivot promised in beat 134.
storyboard.addedInformation: Jack first because he is the active partner in this moment of resistance.

storyboard.claim: They leave fake love notes from the disgusting fictional Bula in Julian's locker.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack holding a note with a happy grin — the prank in its literal form.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The specific weapon in their counterattack, shown physically.
storyboard.addedInformation: Notes icon is literal (actual paper notes), callout names the joke target.

callout.text: SHOWS THEY ARENT JUST PASSIVE VICTIMS

storyboard.claim: The Bula prank is brilliant — it proves they aren't passive victims waiting for a savior.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack and Auggie celebrating — real joy, not performance.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Narrator's verdict on the Bula gambit — names what it proves about their character.
storyboard.addedInformation: Celebrate action is earned here; it is one of the few genuinely joyful beats in the chunk.

storyboard.claim: They use humor and absurdity to reclaim power — a great moment of resilience — but the deeper shadow is Julian's parents.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie and Jack talking happily — the resilience — before the pivot to the parents.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the Bula section and pivots toward Julian's family as the deeper cause.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the pivot to 'shadow looming' is only signaled by narration, not yet staged.

storyboard.claim: Julian's mother took the class photo and used Photoshop to meticulously erase Auggie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Isabel (the parent) beside Julian smirking — mother and son, the adult source of the child's behaviour made visible.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: First evidence that Julian's cruelty has a parental source.
storyboard.addedInformation: Isabel added to cast to show it was the mother who edited the photo, not Julian himself.

storyboard.claim: A grown adult woman erasing a child from a class photo — the narrator finds it sickening.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie slumped — the one erased, the victim of an adult's calculated cruelty.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Emotional reaction to the Photoshop revelation — shifts focus to the human cost.
storyboard.addedInformation: Auggie is the subject of the erasure; staging him grounds the abstract outrage.

storyboard.claim: Julian's mother goes further — she pushes the school board to review Auggie's application to Beecher Prep.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie worried and slumped — the institutional pressure on his right to be there.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Escalates from Photoshop to active bureaucratic attack on Auggie's enrollment.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the mother is not on screen — Auggie carries the threat.

storyboard.claim: Defining 'inclusion school' — a school that mixes neurotypical kids with special-needs students.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Tushman explaining in the classroom — the administrator who will rebut the claim.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Provides the definition before Tushman's rebuttal in the next beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the definition is in the narration; the visual only anchors Tushman as the voice of reason.

storyboard.claim: Tushman rightly points out: Auggie has zero developmental or intellectual special needs — he just looks different.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie standing neutral in the classroom — his presence is the whole argument.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers Tushman's rebuttal — the enrollment challenge collapses on its own logic.
storyboard.addedInformation: Auggie's distinctive look carries the visual argument without needing an icon.

storyboard.claim: One host argues Julian is simply a bad seed — the classic inherently-cruel villain archetype.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian smirking — presented as the textbook antagonist the argument is about to dismantle.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the debate about Julian's nature that the next beats will resolve.
storyboard.addedInformation: Smirk (not happy) keeps Julian threatening rather than charming.

callout.text: The inherently cruel thesis deserves a rebuttal

storyboard.claim: Julian as snake-in-the-garden / inherently cruel — and the host's declaration that this is wrong.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian pointing angrily — the image of cruelty the second host is about to challenge.
storyboard.onScreenText: push back as hard as I can
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The pushback declaration sets up the mirror/parenting argument in the next beats.
storyboard.addedInformation: Angry face shows threat; the callout signals the counter-argument is coming.

storyboard.claim: Julian is not a bad seed — he is an exact reflection of his mother's anxieties and prejudices.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian blank-faced (apathy/numbness) — a vessel, not an agent of independent cruelty.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Counter to the 'bad seed' argument — reframes Julian as a product, not a cause.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank face: he has no independent moral content here, which is precisely the argument. Mirror icon avoided — it reads as self-image, not 'reflection of parents' values.'

callout.text: YEAR OLD BOY DOES NOT COME

storyboard.claim: A 10-year-old does not come up with the bureaucratic term 'inclusion school' on his own — it came from his parents.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian blank — a child who is not the origin of the ideas he's acting on.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: First piece of evidence for the 'mirror' thesis — the language test.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank face sustained from beat 146 — the same argument, the same visual state.

storyboard.claim: A 10-year-old also doesn't think to digitally alter a class photograph to erase a classmate — that is an adult's idea.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian holding the photo, blank-faced — the instrument of erasure is in his hands but the idea came from above.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Second piece of evidence — the Photoshop action traced back to its adult origin.
storyboard.addedInformation: Photo icon is literal; blank face repeats the 'vessel not agent' visual.

callout.text: REACTION TO SOMETHING HE DOESNT UNDERSTAND

storyboard.claim: Julian was initially afraid of Auggie — natural but unfortunate — and instead of being guided through it, his parents validated the cruelty.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian afraid facing Auggie — the original reaction — before parents made it worse.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Grants Julian's initial fear as human, then shows where the parenting failed.
storyboard.addedInformation: Afraid face on Julian is rare and important — it rehumanises him before indicting his parents.

callout.text: handed him the wrong answer key

storyboard.claim: Julian failed the moral test because his parents handed him the wrong answer key before he even walked into the room.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian blank — the child who arrived pre-equipped with a wrong moral framework.
storyboard.onScreenText: handed him the wrong answer key
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the thesis of the 'mirror' argument — parental culpability in concrete terms.
storyboard.addedInformation: The metaphor 'answer key' is from the narration; no icon captures it without misreading.

storyboard.claim: The book's sorting mechanism doesn't just test kids in the cafeteria — its gravity extends into the parents' living rooms, exposing moral rot in the adults.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Isabel thinking, worried — a parent figure reckoning with the test they are also taking.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Broadens the argument from Julian's specific parents to all adult bystanders.
storyboard.addedInformation: Isabel is the closest available adult-parent cast member; she stands for all parents implicated.

storyboard.claim: August's reality tests the whole system — and now the story moves back to the family, to Via.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie standing — the fixed moral centre around whom everything else orbits.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the Julian/parents section and pivots to the family dynamic.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the transition to Via is only in the narration; the visual stays on Auggie.

storyboard.claim: Via's story may be the most emotionally complex — the psychological toll on the invisible sibling.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Via slumped alone in her bedroom — the invisible one, weighted down.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: First beat anchoring the Via section after the pivot in beat 152.
storyboard.addedInformation: Bedroom set matches 'via_bedroom' from the story-bible.

storyboard.claim: A few days after spring break: mom discovers Via has been hiding her involvement in a high-school play from the whole family.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Via worried in her bedroom — the secret about to be uncovered.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets the scene for the confrontation that follows.
storyboard.addedInformation: The bedroom set with theatre posters (story-bible) makes the hidden play visible in the background.

storyboard.claim: Mom is furious — you can hear them screaming at each other through the bedroom walls.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Via and Isabel facing each other angry, both talking — the fight made physical.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The confrontation erupts immediately after the secret is discovered.
storyboard.addedInformation: Via first in cast — this scene is ultimately about her pain, not Isabel's anger.

storyboard.claim: Isabel calls Via moody and secretive; Via screams back defending herself — 'What is so wrong with my not telling you?'
storyboard.concreteVisual: Via pointing angrily at Isabel — the accusation returned, the eruption visible.
storyboard.onScreenText: What's wrong with not telling you?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The screaming fight escalates to direct accusation — Via's perspective front and centre.
storyboard.addedInformation: Callout is Via's own words from the narration — her voice, not a label.

callout.text: DONT YOU WANT US TO SEE

storyboard.claim: Via erupts: 'No, actually, I don't' want you there — revealing the hidden cost of orbiting Auggie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Via alone, pointing, angry — the single raw syllable of refusal.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The peak of Via's eruption before the narrator explains what it means.
storyboard.addedInformation: The three-word callout is Via's exact words — the shortest, most loaded line in the scene.

storyboard.claim: The scene reveals the concept of 'glass children' — siblings of children with severe needs whose parents look right through them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Via slumped alone — the glass child, present but unseen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the psychological concept the Via eruption just demonstrated.
storyboard.addedInformation: No icon maps to 'glass children' without misreading — staging Via as invisible is the picture.

storyboard.claim: Glass children get their name because parents look right through them to the child who needs urgent care — Via has done this for a decade.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Via slumped in the foreground, Auggie behind — she is there but the family's attention flows past her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines glass children with the exact visual the name implies — Via in front, Auggie behind.
storyboard.addedInformation: Auggie's presence makes the 'looking through to Auggie' spatial relationship legible.
